title: Illinois Signs Nation's Strictest AI Safety Law, Requiring Annual Audits of Frontier Models
excerpt: Governor Pritzker signs the Artificial Intelligence Safety Measures Act, making Illinois the first state to mandate independent third-party audits of the largest AI systems.
body:
• Illinois Governor JB Pritzker signed the Artificial Intelligence Safety Measures Act into law on July 6, establishing the nation's strictest safety requirements for frontier AI models.
  • The law requires annual independent third-party audits — a first for any state — for AI companies reporting more than $500 million in annual revenue.
  • Companies must report critical safety incidents within 72 hours, or 24 hours if the incident creates a risk of death or serious physical harm. Penalties reach up to $3 million per repeat violation.
  • OpenAI and Anthropic both endorsed the bill; the law takes effect January 1, 2027.

What the Law Does

Illinois Governor JB Pritzker signed the Artificial Intelligence Safety Measures Act into law on July 6, making the state the first in the nation to require independent third-party audits of the most advanced AI systems. The law targets frontier AI models — the largest and most powerful systems — developed by companies with more than $500 million in annual revenue.

Under the new statute, covered developers must publish a framework detailing how they identify and mitigate catastrophic risks, submit to annual audits by independent evaluators without financial conflicts of interest, and report critical safety incidents to the state within 72 hours. If an incident creates a risk of death or serious physical harm, the reporting window narrows to 24 hours.

"As AI systems become more powerful and the federal government is unwilling to step in, states have a responsibility to protect our people from the dangers of AI while still harnessing the unique potential of the technology."

— JB Pritzker, Governor of Illinois

Bipartisan Support, Industry Backing

The bill, Senate Bill 315, passed unanimously in the Illinois House and 52–5 in the Senate. It drew endorsements from both OpenAI and Anthropic — a notable alignment between two companies that had previously clashed over AI regulation in the state. OpenAI had pushed a separate bill that would have shielded AI companies from lawsuits over large-scale harms. Anthropic opposed that measure, which has since stalled.

Cesar Fernandez, head of state and local government relations for Anthropic, said the law "makes Illinois the first state to pair AI transparency requirements with independent verification, an important step toward the accountability this technology demands."

The law defines catastrophic events as incidents resulting in 50 or more deaths or $1 billion or more in damage — thresholds designed to focus the requirements on genuinely existential risks rather than routine technical failures.

A Growing State-Level Movement

Illinois joins California and New York in building a state-level AI regulatory framework. Together, the three states hold about 20% of the U.S. population but cover an estimated 40% of the AI market by revenue, giving their regulations outsized influence even without federal action.

The law borrows elements from California's and New York's AI transparency statutes but goes further with its audit mandate. The audit requirement takes effect January 1, 2028, giving companies roughly 18 months to prepare. Penalties for violations reach up to $3 million per repeat offense.

The law also creates confidential reporting channels and whistleblower protections for employees at AI companies who raise safety concerns — provisions that could have particular resonance given recent high-profile departures of safety-focused researchers from OpenAI and other labs.

What's Next

Federal AI legislation remains stalled in Congress, leaving states to fill the regulatory vacuum. The Illinois law's passage suggests the momentum is building for a de facto national standard set by the states that host the largest AI companies and their customers.

For the AI industry, the practical question is whether compliance frameworks built for California, New York, and Illinois can be extended nationally — or whether a growing patchwork of state laws will create the kind of regulatory complexity that eventually forces federal action. Industry groups have called for harmonization, but with no federal bill on the horizon, the state-by-state approach appears set to continue.
